Header:

- Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Luis Hernandez (Redwood SE), Ruth Carter (Praxis Lead Engineer), Devon Kim (Praxis PM), Anika Rao (Praxis Security)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Friday afternoon. I'm Maya from Redwood — AE — and I'll hand over to Luis who will run through a live lab. But first quick intros?
[00:12] Ruth: Hey, I'm Ruth, lead engineer at Praxis, working on our payments reconciler.
[00:17] Devon: Devon, product manager, coordinating the POC.
[00:20] Anika: Anika from security, I'll be validating compliance and network setup.
[00:24] Luis: Great, thanks. Quick agenda — 1) show SDK quickstarts for Python and TypeScript, 2) auth patterns and sandbox vs prod, 3) console walk and Optimize hints, 4) Q&A and next steps. We'll do live runs on the Python side and paste some TS snippets.
[00:40] Maya: Quick context — Praxis said you want to add summarization and a downstream routing microservice. You're concerned about latency and cost; correct?
[00:47] Ruth: Yes, mostly latency under 300ms tail and cost per 1M tokens. Also we need clear secrets handling in CI.
[00:55] Devon: And a short timeline — proof-of-concept within 3 weeks.
[00:58] Luis: Ok perfect. I'll start by opening the console — note, the actual console shown is a demo project; your sandbox will look the same.
[01:12] [screen share] Luis: Here is Projects -> Sandbox- Praxis-POC. We recommend creating a project per environment — sandbox, staging, prod. Routes map to service intents; you can pin model versions here. See the quickstart card with SDK snippets.
[01:40] Luis: Now the Python quickstart. Small note on install: pip install redwood-sdk (sometimes transcribed as redwood-skd in auto text).
[01:50] Luis: Code:
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate('Summarize: ' + long_text, model='redwood-2-small', max_tokens=256)
print(resp.text)
[02:10] Ruth: When you say api_key at runtime, do you support role-scoped keys? We cannot put a universal token in CI.
[02:18] Luis: Yes — two recommended patterns. 1) short-lived role-scoped keys minted via the console or an internal service (we can provision an API key with restricted scopes for sandbox). 2) SSO + OIDC flow for server-side workloads; Redwood supports SAML/SCIM for provisioning, and you can integrate single-sign on for human flows.
[02:38] Anika: For the role-scoped keys, where's the credential stored? We use HashiCorp Vault, ideally KMS integration to wrap keys.
[02:45] Maya: Absolutely — Redwood supports KMS integration for key material and you can rotate keys; our Private deployment has HSM options, and hosted supports KMS for customer-managed keys. We'll add the security integration doc.
[02:58] Devon: What's the recommended pattern for CI — ephemeral key or secret manager pull?
[03:05] Luis: Best practice: store long-lived secrets in Vault or GitHub Secrets, then mint ephemeral role-scoped key at build time via an internal service that calls Redwood's token mint endpoint. This keeps the long-lived secret confined to Vault. We have a sample GitHub Actions snippet in the quickstart.
[03:25] Luis: Now I'll run the Python script with a small 200-token summary prompt to demo latency.
[03:38] [live run noise]
[03:42] Luis: Ok it returned — time to first token ~120ms in this sandbox demo; your production numbers may vary by model and region.
[03:52] Ruth: That looks good. How do we measure tail latency in the console?
[03:58] Luis: Console > Observability has per-route token breakdown, P95/P99 latency charts, and token-level cost estimates. You can instrument traces too. We'll show that in a sec.
[04:15] Maya: Also, Redwood Optimize gives batching and caching suggestions based on your call patterns. If you have lots of short completions, batching helps reduce token cost but watch latency SLOs.
[04:30] Ruth: Can you explain cache — prefix cache? We have repetitive prompts when reconciling similar transactions.
[04:36] Luis: We do KV cache / prefix caching — the platform can cache recent prefixes and reuse cached KV caches for continuing conversations; that reduces compute. For stateless calls, prefix caching caches identical prompt hashes. We'll share the Optimize recommendations for your workload later.
[04:50] Anika: On audit logs — does the hosted plan provide redact/PII controls in logs? We can't log full PII to external systems.
[04:56] Maya: Hosted offers configurable logging — you can disable payload logging, only retain event-level metrics, or use Private for full control and on-prem audit trails. We also support field-level redaction in logs.
[05:10] Luis: Switching to TS quickstart — basically the same flow. npm i @redwood/sdk — snippet:
import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/sdk';
const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
const out = await client.generate({ prompt: 'Summarize...', model: 'redwood-2-small', maxTokens: 150 });
console.log(out.text);
[05:35] Devon: For the TS snippet, is there builtin retry/backoff? We have transient network errors in our infra.
[05:42] Luis: SDKs include a retry policy configurable at client init — exponential backoff with jitter; you can override per-call. Also supports streaming token callbacks for real-time UI.
[05:55] Ruth: Streaming is important for our user-facing summary microservice. Does streaming change billing model?
[06:02] Luis: No, billing is per-token generated/consumed; streaming just delivers tokens earlier — cost same. But keep an eye on network throughput.
[06:12] [timestamp noise, brief crosstalk]
[06:18] Luis: Now demo of console observability — routes, model pins, and Optimize hints. See suggested batch size 8 for this workload — because you had many short requests historically in demo dataset. That reduces cost ~40% on the example.
[06:35] Ruth: How do we roll a new model version without downtime?
[06:40] Luis: We have rollout policies — canary deploy to X% of traffic, A/B experiments, and automatic fallback to previous model if latency or error rate crosses thresholds. Very helpful during model swaps.
[06:52] Anika: Regarding network, we have strict egress rules. Can Redwood run in our VPC?
[06:58] Maya: Yes — Redwood Private allows VPC peering or on-prem bundle. For hosted customers we also offer VPC-hosted private connectors in selected regions. We'll capture your network CIDR and exchange network docs.
[07:12] Devon: About quotas and rate limits — we might need bursts for batch jobs. How does Dedicated compare?
[07:18] Luis: Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput with burst capacity options. Hosted has burst policies but not guaranteed throughput. For heavy batch jobs, Dedicated with autoscaling policies is better. We'll scope this in the POC if you expect sustained high throughput.
[07:36] Maya: Quick demo of env var patterns — we recommend REDWOOD_API_KEY for app servers, REDWOOD_SANDBOX_KEY for CI that only has generation permissions, and REDWOOD_AUDIT_MODE env flag off for prod to reduce payload logs.
[07:52] Ruth: Can the sandbox key be made to expire in 24 hours?
[07:56] Luis: Yes — when minting role-scoped keys via the console or API you can set TTLs. We'll provision a 7-day sandbox key by default and then you can rotate.
[08:08] [screen share: GitHub Actions snippet] Luis: Example CI snippet — checkout, read secrets from Vault or GitHub Secrets, call internal mint endpoint, set REDWOOD_API_KEY then run tests.
[08:28] Devon: Sounds good. For our POC, we'll run a local benchmark with 512-token sequences. Do you have a recommended harness?
[08:36] Luis: We have a simple harness in the repo: loadtest.py which issues async calls with adjustable concurrency and token lengths; we'll drop it into your sandbox project.
[08:46] Ruth: One more security nit — we need to ensure logs are stored in our S3 with server-side encryption and that Redwood's logs can be forwarded.
[08:54] Anika: Also need SOC2 type II evidence and a data processing addendum.
[08:58] Maya: We'll attach the SOC2 report and DPA; for logs you can forward observability events to your S3 or SIEM; for hosted we provide a log-forwarding integration.
[09:10] [pause — demo continues]
[09:15] Luis: Now I want to show Optimize suggestions in the Console — hint: enable prefix cache for reconciliation flows, and set a batching policy with full and partial timeouts to keep latency within 300ms but get some batching benefit.
[09:35] Ruth: Will batch grouping break request-level tracing? We need to tie tokens back to original request IDs.
[09:42] Luis: No, Redwood attaches mapping metadata so you can trace per-request even if batched. The console shows expanded traces and you can instrument with headers.
[09:55] Devon: Any hard limits on token size for embeddings vs generation?
[10:00] Luis: Embeddings typically limit input to ~4096 tokens depending on model; generation max depends on combined prompt+response. We'll include model-specific limits in the quickstart doc.
[10:11] Anika: For compliance, can we request IP allowlist and dedicated logs retention?
[10:15] Maya: Yes for enterprise plans. Log retention and IP allowlists are configurable — we'll include that in the enterprise checklist.
[10:25] Luis: I'm going to run a small stream to show partials — streaming callback gives UI time to render.
[10:34] [live stream demo — partials appear]
[10:42] Ruth: Nice. Can we get the SDK sample integrated into our Node service with minimal code changes?
[10:48] Luis: Yes — we have middlewares and adapters for Express/Koa and a lightweight shim if you want to swap providers later.
[10:56] Devon: Switching topics — will the billing show per-route cost so we can chargeback?
[11:02] Maya: Yes — per-route and per-token breakdown, exportable as CSV. You can also tag routes and set budgets per-project.
[11:12] Anika: Last question, do you support customer-managed keys for hosted plans?
[11:17] Maya: Yes — optional KMS integration for managed encryption keys; Private supports HSM for more rigorous controls.
[11:26] Luis: Ok, last bit — I'll paste the repo link and the quickstart doc in chat: https://docs.redwood.ai/quickstart and a sandbox project link (demo-only) https://console.redwood.ai/p/projects/sandbox-praxis (these are placeholders).
[11:45] Maya: Recap and next steps: we'll provision sandbox creds, share quickstart + CI patterns, attach SOC2 and network checklist, and schedule a POC scoping call on Dec 8.
[11:58] Ruth: Thanks — this was very helpful. We'll prepare sample prompts and an SLO doc.
[12:03] Devon: We'll coordinate calendar invites for Dec 8.
[12:08] Anika: I'll send specific security controls we need attached to the invite.
[12:14] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and the sandbox key.
[12:20] [call ends]
